```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
pal <- c(navy = "#2b3a67", teal = "#2a9d8f", orange = "#e76f51",
         gold = "#e9c46a", grey = "#bbbbbb")
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))
set.seed(11)
```

## This afternoon {.center}

We are not running any software.

. . .

By the end you should be able to say, in your own words, where each number in a
count table came from.

## A sequencer returns text

```
@A00984:412:HTKJ7DSXX:1:1101:2645:1000 1:N:0:ACTGAGCG
TACGTAGGGTGCGAGCGTTGTCCGGATTTATTGGGCGTAAAGCGCGCGCAGGCGGTTTGTT
+
FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFF
```

. . .

Millions of these per sample. A name, a sequence, and a quality score per base.

. . .

Everything that follows is an attempt to answer one question: **what was in the
tube, and how much of it?**

## Not every base is trustworthy

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.3
set.seed(7)
tibble(cycle = 1:150) |>
  mutate(q = 38 - 0.00035 * cycle^2 - rnorm(150, 0, 0.4),
         lo = q - 4.5, hi = pmin(q + 2.5, 41)) |>
  ggplot(aes(cycle, q)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = pal[["teal"]], alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(colour = pal[["navy"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20, linetype = 2, colour = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 20, y = 17.5, label = "a common trimming threshold",
           size = 4.2, colour = pal[["orange"]], hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "position in the read", y = "quality score") +
  ylim(10, 42)
```

Quality falls along the read. Before anything else, somebody trimmed these.

## The decisions already made for you {.smaller}

By the time you receive a count table, someone has chosen:

::: {.incremental}
- where to trim each read
- which samples were too poor to keep
- which reference to compare against
- what to do with reads that matched more than one thing
- what to do with reads that matched nothing
:::

. . .

None of those choices are in the table. All of them changed its contents.

. . .

Ask who made them.

## Two experiments, two paths, one destination

```{r}
#| fig-width: 15
#| fig-height: 6
steps <- tribble(
  ~path, ~step, ~label,
  "16S", 1, "cervicovaginal\nswab",
  "16S", 2, "amplify the\n16S V3-V4 region",
  "16S", 3, "sequence",
  "16S", 4, "denoise into\nexact sequences",
  "16S", 5, "classify against\na reference",
  "16S", 6, "counts per\nspecies",
  "RNA", 1, "cervicovaginal\nswab",
  "RNA", 2, "capture mRNA,\nmake cDNA",
  "RNA", 3, "sequence",
  "RNA", 4, "align to the\nhuman genome",
  "RNA", 5, "count reads\nper gene model",
  "RNA", 6, "counts per\ngene"
) |>
  mutate(y = if_else(path == "16S", 2, 1),
         fill = case_when(step == 6 ~ pal[["navy"]],
                          path == "16S" ~ pal[["teal"]],
                          TRUE ~ pal[["orange"]]))

ggplot(steps, aes(step, y)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = step, xend = step + 0.98, y = y, yend = y),
               data = steps |> filter(step < 6),
               colour = pal[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.8,
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = fill), width = 0.86, height = 0.62, colour = "white", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), colour = "white", size = 3.8, lineheight = 0.95,
            fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(2, 1), labels = c("16S", "RNA-seq"), limits = c(0.5, 2.5)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_void(base_size = 16) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "grey25", hjust = 1,
                                   margin = margin(r = 10)))
```

Different biology, different software, same final object.

## 16S: one gene, every bacterium {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
The 16S ribosomal RNA gene is in every bacterium, and parts of it differ between
species.

::: {.incremental}
- amplify one variable region with PCR
- sequence only that amplicon
- group identical sequences together
- look each one up in a reference database
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(conserved = 0.15 + 0.1 * sin(x * 3),
         variable = if_else(x > 3 & x < 5 | x > 7 & x < 8.5, 0.9, 0.15)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x)) +
  geom_area(aes(y = variable), fill = pal[["teal"]], alpha = 0.85) +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 1.05, label = "V3", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 7.75, y = 1.05, label = "V4", size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.33, label = "conserved", size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
  labs(x = "position along the 16S gene", y = "variation between species") +
  ylim(0, 1.15) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

## PCR is not a neutral copier

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4.2
tibble(
  species = c("species A", "species B", "species C", "species D"),
  truth = c(40, 30, 20, 10),
  observed = c(26, 41, 11, 22)
) |>
  pivot_longer(-species, names_to = "what", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(what = recode(what, truth = "cells in the tube", observed = "reads you get back")) |>
  ggplot(aes(species, pct, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`cells in the tube` = pal[["grey"]],
                               `reads you get back` = pal[["teal"]])) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "percent", fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

Primers bind some templates better than others, and 16S copy number varies
between species. The ordering can change.

## Grouping reads: ASVs and OTUs {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
Two sequences differing by one base. Same organism, or two?

::: {.incremental}
- **OTUs** cluster anything within, say, 3% of each other. Robust, blunt.
- **ASVs** model the sequencing error process and resolve exact sequences.
  Sharper, and sensitive to the error model being right.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4
set.seed(12)
tibble(x = c(rnorm(60, 2, 0.35), rnorm(40, 4, 0.35), rnorm(8, 3, 1.2)),
       y = c(rnorm(60, 2, 0.35), rnorm(40, 3.4, 0.35), rnorm(8, 2.6, 1.2)),
       kind = c(rep("abundant variant", 60), rep("abundant variant", 40),
                rep("error reads", 8))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, colour = kind, size = kind)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`abundant variant` = pal[["navy"]],
                                 `error reads` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(2.6, 1.4)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  theme_void(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
:::
:::

## Then you look it up, and often cannot tell {.smaller}

The variable region you sequenced is short. Some species are identical across it.

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  `what the classifier can say` = c("Lactobacillus crispatus",
                                    "Gardnerella, but which species is ambiguous",
                                    "family only",
                                    "bacteria"),
  `how our table names it` = c("lactobacillus_crispatus",
                              "gardnerella_swidsinskii_leopoldii",
                              "prevotella_sp_1",
                              "dropped")
) |> knitr::kable()
```

. . .

Two of our 220 row names are honest admissions of uncertainty. Read your row
names before you interpret them.

## What a 16S count means

A cell in the species table is: **the number of amplicon reads in this sample
that matched this species.**

. . .

That is not the number of bacteria. Between the cell and the count sit

::: {.incremental}
- how many copies of the 16S gene that species carries
- how well the primers bind to it
- how completely the cells lysed
- how deeply the sample was sequenced
:::

## RNA-seq: every gene, one organism {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.incremental}
- pull out messenger RNA
- copy it to cDNA and fragment it
- sequence the fragments
- find where each fragment belongs in the genome
- count fragments overlapping each gene
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
reads <- tibble(start = runif(26, 0, 9), y = rep(1:13, each = 2) * 0.07 + 0.25)
tibble(x = 0) |>
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 10, ymin = 0.05, ymax = 0.17,
           fill = pal[["grey"]]) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = c(1, 4.2, 7.5), xmax = c(2.6, 6, 9.2), ymin = 0.05, ymax = 0.17,
           fill = pal[["navy"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.8, y = 0.01, label = "exon", size = 4, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_segment(data = reads, aes(x = start, xend = start + 0.75, y = y, yend = y),
               colour = pal[["orange"]], linewidth = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "position along the gene", y = NULL) +
  xlim(0, 10) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())
```
:::
:::

## What an RNA-seq count means

A cell in the gene table is: **the number of fragments in this sample assigned
to this gene.**

. . .

Also not a molecule count. Between the transcript and the count sit

::: {.incremental}
- how long the gene is
- how well the capture chemistry worked
- whether the read could be placed uniquely
- how deeply the sample was sequenced
:::

## One swab, two experiments {.smaller}

A cervicovaginal swab contains human cells and bacteria together.

::: {.incremental}
- The 16S run amplifies a bacterial gene, so human material is mostly ignored.
- The RNA-seq run captures polyadenylated RNA, which is mostly human.
- Neither is pure. Both are the same swab.
:::

. . .

That is why we can pair the two tables sample by sample at all.

## Reads that could have come from anywhere

```{r}
#| fig-width: 13
#| fig-height: 4
tibble(x = 0) |>
  ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = c(0.5, 5.5), xmax = c(3.5, 8.5), ymin = 1, ymax = 1.5,
           fill = pal[["navy"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = c(2, 7), y = 1.75, label = c("gene A", "gene B"), size = 4.6) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 4.3, xmax = 4.9, ymin = 0.45, ymax = 0.75,
           fill = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 4.6, y = 0.2, label = "one read, two homes", size = 4.4,
           colour = pal[["orange"]]) +
  annotate("segment", x = 4.6, xend = c(2.6, 6.6), y = 0.8, yend = 0.95,
           colour = pal[["orange"]], linetype = 2) +
  xlim(0, 9) + ylim(0, 2) +
  theme_void()
```

Gene families and repeats produce reads that fit several genes. Counting them
once, twice or not at all are three different tables.

## Counts, not TPM, for testing {.smaller}

You will see expression reported as TPM, FPKM or RPKM. Those divide by gene
length so you can compare genes within a sample.

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- Good for: "is gene A higher than gene B in this sample?"
- Wrong for: the statistical tests we run on Tuesday
:::

. . .

Those tests need raw counts, because they model counting noise. Hand them
normalised values and they will believe the noise is smaller than it is.

## The compositional problem, drawn

```{r}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 4.6
d <- tibble(
  sample = rep(c("sample 1", "sample 2"), each = 3),
  feature = rep(c("A", "B", "C"), 2),
  absolute = c(100, 100, 100, 100, 100, 700)
) |>
  group_by(sample) |>
  mutate(relative = absolute / sum(absolute)) |>
  ungroup()

p_abs <- ggplot(d, aes(sample, absolute, fill = feature)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "what is really there", x = NULL, y = "cells") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("teal", "navy", "orange")]))
p_rel <- ggplot(d, aes(sample, relative, fill = feature)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(title = "what the count table shows", x = NULL, y = "share of reads") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("teal", "navy", "orange")]))
p_abs + p_rel
```

A and B never changed. In the table, both appear to fall by more than half.

## Which bites both tables {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- It is severe in 16S, where one species routinely holds 90% of the reads.
- It is milder in RNA-seq, where no single gene dominates, but it is still
  there.
- It is why "relative abundance went down" is not the same claim as "there was
  less of it".
:::

. . .

Without a spike-in or an absolute measurement, you cannot tell the two apart.

## What to demand from your sequencing facility {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}
- the raw reads, not just the table
- the exact reference and version used
- which samples failed and were re-run
- which plate, run and lane each sample sat on
- the negative and positive controls, with their counts
:::

. . .

That last one catches contamination, and almost nobody asks for it.

## What goes wrong, in practice {.smaller}

| problem | how you notice |
|---|---|
| contamination from reagents | the same taxa in your negative controls |
| low-biomass samples | tiny library sizes, odd composition |
| index hopping between samples | a trace of everything in everything |
| a batch effect | samples cluster by run, not by biology |

: {tbl-colwidths="[42,58]"}

. . .

Three of those four are invisible unless somebody recorded the metadata.

## The sentence to remember {.center}

A count table is **not** a measurement of how much was there.

. . .

It is a measurement of how much was there, **relative to everything else in that
tube**, multiplied by how hard we looked.

## Which is why every analysis starts the same way

::: {.incremental}
1. How deeply was each sample sequenced?
2. Which features are we even able to see?
3. Only then: does anything differ between groups?
:::

. . .

Tomorrow morning is step 1 and step 2, on both tables at once.

## One more label we will keep {.smaller}

Our gene table was produced in **two sequencing batches**.

. . .

We could have hidden that. We left it in, because on Wednesday you will measure
how much of the table it explains, and the answer is uncomfortable.

. . .

Keep every technical label your sequencing facility gives you. You cannot check
for a problem you did not write down.

## On your feet {.center}

Put the laptops away.
